analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or cutting benefits because someone received grief counseling.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee on May 4-5, 2009, and never received a vote or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Public Health Service Act to stop health insurers selling individual-market policies from using a person's receipt of grief counseling as a reason to deny them coverage, deny continued enrollment, or reduce their benefits. The rules would apply to individual-market coverage from the date of enactment. The bill was introduced in May 2009 and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health insurance and have sought grief counseling — for example after the death of a spouse, child, or parent — would be protected from being turned down for a policy, losing their policy, or having counseling-related needs carved out of their benefits. It also supports bereaved families generally by removing an insurance penalty for seeking mental health support after a loss.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Individual-market buyers who sought grief counseling

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits insurers in the individual market from establishing or maintaining eligibility rules based on a person's receipt of grief counseling at any time, meaning they could not use it as a reason to deny or discontinue enrollment.

It also prohibits insurers from reducing the benefits covered, or offered for coverage, on the basis that an individual received grief counseling, protecting bereaved people from benefit discrimination.
The prohibition applies to individual-market coverage offered, sold, issued, renewed, in effect, or operated on or after the date of enactment, so it would take effect immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance companies selling individual-market policies would bear the cost of not being able to screen out or limit coverage for people who have received grief counseling, and premiums across the individual market would absorb whatever risk that adds.

drawbacks.text: The bill addresses a relatively narrow slice of insurance discrimination: it applies only to the individual market, and only to the single factor of grief counseling, so people facing similar discrimination for other forms of mental health care would not be covered by this bill.

Insurers and critics of coverage mandates argue that restrictions on underwriting in the individual market raise premiums for everyone in that market, since insurers can no longer price or screen for conditions they consider higher risk; the bill does not address how those added costs are absorbed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the small group of people who could be denied or downgraded coverage because they sought counseling after a loss, the protection is real and valuable. The protection is narrow — one trigger, in one market — and insurers would spread the added risk into individual-market premiums, a cost that is real but modest for a single mental-health factor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee the week it was introduced, got no cosponsors, and was never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Deborah Halvorson introduced the bill on May 4, 2009.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
The bill attracted no cosponsors over its life.
No further action was taken after the subcommittee referral; the bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers selling individual-market policies are better off, because they never faced a rule barring them from using grief counseling as a basis for denying or limiting coverage. Bereaved people who buy their own insurance got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Individual-market insurers; bereaved buyers got nothing

for.name: Rep. Deborah Halvorson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee; it was her only direct action on it and it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Henry Waxman (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out or scheduled action on it during the Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 5, 2009, and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no vote or coalition ever formed and the partisan shape of the issue was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped individual-market insurers of the ability to deny coverage, drop enrollees, or cut benefits based on receipt of grief counseling. Its death left their underwriting discretion intact. For ordinary people, that discretion is a cost: it allows coverage decisions to turn on bereavement-related care.
